title: Subtree Sums While the Values Change

concept.title: Flatten the tree with a DFS order so that every subtree is a range, then use a Fenwick tree
body: We need two operations on a tree, many times: **change** the value of one node, and ask for the **sum of the values in a subtree**. Recomputing the subtree sum walks the whole subtree, O(n) per question. The trick is to turn the tree into an **array**.

Number the nodes in the order of a **depth-first (pre-order) walk**: the *entry time* `tin[v]`. All nodes of the subtree of `v` get **consecutive** numbers: from `tin[v]` to `tin[v] + size[v] - 1`. This is the *Euler tour* idea. So "sum of the subtree of `v`" is "sum of the array from `tin[v]` to `tin[v] + size[v] - 1`", and "change the value of `v`" is "change one array cell".

A range sum with point changes is the job of a **Fenwick tree** (binary indexed tree): an array `bit` where `bit[i]` stores the sum of a block of cells ending at `i`, whose length is the lowest set bit of `i`.

body.code:
def update(pos, delta):                  # add delta to the cell pos (1-based)
    while pos <= n:
        bit[pos] += delta
        pos += pos & -pos

def prefix(pos):                         # the sum of the cells 1..pos
    total = 0
    while pos > 0:
        total += bit[pos]
        pos -= pos & -pos
    return total

# subtree sum of v:  prefix(tin[v] + size[v] - 1) - prefix(tin[v] - 1)

body: Both operations take O(log n). The DFS order is made without recursion (a stack: pop a node, number it, push its children), and the sizes come from the breadth-first order walked backwards. The sums reach 2 * 10^13 in absolute value, so use 64-bit integers.

statement: A tree with `n` nodes is given by the parent of each node (0 for the root), and every node has a starting value. Then `q` operations follow. `add v x` adds `x` to the value of the node `v`. `sum v 0` asks for the sum of the current values of all nodes in the subtree of `v` (the node `v` and everything below it); the second number is 0 and must be ignored. Print the answer to every `sum`.
inputFormat: The first line has `n`, the number of nodes (numbered 1 to n).
The second line has `n` numbers: for each node its parent, and 0 for the root.
The third line has `n` numbers: the starting value of every node.
The fourth line has `q`, the number of operations.

Each of the next `q` lines has an operation and two numbers: `add v x` adds `x` to the value of the node `v`; `sum v 0` asks for the sum of the values in the subtree of `v` (the second number of `sum` is 0 and must be ignored).
outputFormat: One line for every `sum` operation, in order.
constraints: The numbers describe one tree: exactly one node has the parent 0, and following parents always reaches it.
A parent can have a larger number than its child.
The tree can be a long path (depth up to n - 1).

examples.note: The whole tree sums to 15; after adding 10 to node 4 the subtree of 2 (nodes 2, 4, 5) sums to 2 + 14 + 5 = 21; the subtree of 3 is just 3.

hints: Number the nodes in a depth-first order; every subtree is then a block of consecutive numbers.
The block of v is from tin[v] to tin[v] + size[v] - 1.
Keep the values in a Fenwick tree: a point update and a prefix sum both take O(log n).

explanation: A stack-based depth-first walk numbers the nodes so that every subtree is a block of consecutive numbers; a Fenwick tree over these numbers supports changing one value and summing a block in O(log n).
solution.complexity: Time O((n + q) log n), space O(n).
